analysis.one_liner: Restores federal preapproval of voting changes in states and counties with recent records of voting rights violations.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Voting Rights Amendment Act of 2019, with 20 cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court struck down the old formula for deciding which states needed federal preapproval of voting changes, this bill would have written a new formula based on recent voting rights violations. Covered states and counties would need Justice Department or court sign-off before changing election rules, would have to post public notices of polling place and district changes, and voters would find it easier to sue over discriminatory voting practices. The bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — particularly minority voters in states and counties with recent records of voting rights violations — would gain: federal preapproval of election changes would return, local governments would have to publicly announce polling place and rule changes, individual voters would get new standing to sue, federal election observers could be sent to more places, and courts would have clearer grounds to block discriminatory voting changes before an election.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates preclearance — advance federal approval from the Justice Department or a federal court — for any state with five or more voting rights violations in the previous 15 years (at least one by the state itself), and for counties or subdivisions with three or more violations or one violation plus persistently very low minority turnout [S2, S3]

Requires states and larger localities to publicly announce changes to voting rules within 48 hours and to post data on polling place locations, machines, and poll workers before federal elections, so voters can see last-minute changes [S3]

Expands who can go to court: any aggrieved voter, not just the Attorney General, could seek relief against discriminatory voting practices, and courts must weigh the hardship to voters against the hardship to the government when deciding whether to block a change before an election [S3]
Expands the Justice Department's authority to send federal election observers, including to enforce bilingual voting requirements where complaints of likely violations are received [S3]

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments with records of voting rights violations would bear the cost: they would need Justice Department or court preapproval before changing election rules, publish public notices of every voting change within 48 hours, and disclose polling place resources and district demographic data.

drawbacks.text: The formula is backward-looking and litigious: a jurisdiction escapes coverage simply by staying below the violation count, and states argue that subjecting routine election administration to federal preapproval intrudes on state authority over elections [S3]

The bill carves out photo ID laws: objections and violations based solely on a photo identification requirement do not count toward triggering coverage, which supporters offered as a compromise but which leaves a common contested voting practice outside the trigger [S3]

Covered jurisdictions would bear real administrative costs — 48-hour public notice of every voting change, pre-election publication of polling place resources, and preapproval waits that can delay changes they consider necessary [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give voters concrete, enforceable protections — a workable preclearance formula after the courts struck down the old one, public notice of voting changes, broader standing to sue, and federal observers — at a real but limited cost to the states and counties it covers: compliance paperwork and loss of unilateral control over election changes. Its main weaknesses are the photo ID carve-out and a formula that turns on past court findings, which some covered states would contest in court. On balance the protections for voters outweigh the administrative burden, but the burden is genuine and the compromise provisions were hard-fought.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its civil rights subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress and never got a markup or a vote, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 14, 2019 by Rep. Sensenbrenner, a senior Republican and longtime author of Voting Rights Act renewals, with 20 cosponsors from both parties
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on May 3, 2019 was referred to its Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee
No markup, vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action is the May 2019 subcommittee referral
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no vote ever taken in either chamber

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local jurisdictions that would otherwise face renewed federal review of their voting changes are better off, since no new coverage formula took effect. Voters in places with records of voting discrimination gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Jurisdictions that avoided federal voting oversight

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 14 of 231 House Democrats and 6 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored, led by a senior Republican — but the Democratic-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill after referring it to a subcommittee.

industries.note: The bill would put any state with five or more voting rights violations in the prior 15 years back under federal preapproval, and would require all jurisdictions to publish polling place and district changes — an administrative cost and a loss of discretion over election rules. Because the bill's protections for voters come directly at the expense of these governments' autonomy, their interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Civil rights litigation and voting rights advocacy organizations
industries.note: By letting any aggrieved voter sue and easing the standard for preliminary injunctions, the bill would generate more voting rights litigation against state and local practices. Election law attorneys and civil rights organizations stand to gain work and standing; the public gains a remedy in the same measure.
